Most of the Mid-Lower Jurassic samples we studied exhibited similar demagnetization behav- ior to those of the stratigraphic equivalents from the Sichuan Basin (see Enkin, 19901, and are characterized by weak magnetization and erratic direction. Nevertheless, utilization of PCA and SCGCI techniques has determined a mean direc- tion from eight sites from the lower Jurassic, which marginally passes the fold and reversal tests. Introduction The North China (Sine-Korean) Block (NCB) and the South China (Yang&e) Block (SCB) are the two major cratons that compose the eastern part of China. They are sutured together by the E-W-trending Qinling fold belt, yet there is at present no consensus on the timing of their amal- gamation into the present configuration. Esti- mates on the age of suturing range from Devo- nian to Early Jurassic primarily on geologic grounds (Klimetz, 1983; Zhang et al., 1984; Mat- tauer et al., 1985; Sengor, 1985; Hsu et al., 1987). Increasing paleomagnetic data, however, appear to favor a younger age for the final

Esti- mates on the age of suturing range from Devo- nian to Early Jurassic primarily on geologic grounds (Klimetz, 1983; Zhang et al., 1984; Mat- tauer et al., 1985; Sengor, 1985; Hsu et al., 1987). Increasing paleomagnetic data, however, appear to favor a younger age for the final suturing event. For example, the Late Permian and Trias- sic paleomagnetic poles for both blocks are statis- tically different (McElhinny et al., 1981; Lin et al., 1985; Opdyke et al., 1986; Zhao and Coe, 1989; Steiner et al., 1989; Yang et al., 1991a1, whereas the Cretaceous paleopoles for both are virtually indistinguishable within paleomagnetic uncertainties (Kent et al., 1986; Lee et al., 1987; Enkin et al., 1991a,b). The time of the coales- cence of the NCB and SCB into their present configuration thus seems to be narrowed down by paleomagnetic constraints to the Jurassic. Introduction The North China (Sine-Korean) Block (NCB) and the South China (Yang&e) Block (SCB) are the two major cratons that compose the eastern part of China. They are sutured together by the E-W-trending Qinling fold belt, yet there is at present no consensus on the timing of their amal- gamation into the present configuration. Esti- mates on the age of suturing range from Devo- nian to Early Jurassic primarily on geologic grounds (Klimetz, 1983; Zhang et al., 1984; Mat- tauer et al., 1985; Sengor, 1985; Hsu et al., 1987). Increasing paleomagnetic data, however, appear to favor a younger age for the final

Esti- mates on the age of suturing range from Devo- nian to Early Jurassic primarily on geologic grounds (Klimetz, 1983; Zhang et al., 1984; Mat- tauer et al., 1985; Sengor, 1985; Hsu et al., 1987). Increasing paleomagnetic data, however, appear to favor a younger age for the final suturing event. For example, the Late Permian and Trias- sic paleomagnetic poles for both blocks are statis- tically different (McElhinny et al., 1981; Lin et al., 1985; Opdyke et al., 1986; Zhao and Coe, 1989; Steiner et al., 1989; Yang et al., 1991a1, whereas the Cretaceous paleopoles for both are virtually indistinguishable within paleomagnetic uncertainties (Kent et al., 1986; Lee et al., 1987; Enkin et al., 1991a,b). The time of the coales- cence of the NCB and SCB into their present configuration thus seems to be narrowed down by paleomagnetic constraints to the Jurassic. There- fore, Jurassic paleomagnetic data becomes criti- cal in timing this event. Tectonophysics, 201 (spec. sect.): 1-16. New palaeomagnetic results from the ca. 1300 Ma Gardar lava succession within the Erikstjord Formation of South Greenland are presented. This study incorporates stepwise thermal demagnetisation of 256 samples from 66 lava flows from all three lava groups in this formation, accompanied by principal component analysis. The results identify two complete reversals (N + R + NJ in the upper lava group and two (R -+ N and N -+ RI in the lower group, with a possible palaeoexcursjon in the lower group. A minimum of two further reversals are predicted in the time interval represented by the sandstone units intercalated with the lava flows. Both complete reversals in the upper group exhibit inclination asymmetries of 30 O. This degree of asymmetry is satisfied by a geomagnetic field model equivalent to a dipole axially offset by 570 km.

Four of these reversals, within the upper lava group, showed an asymme- try of ca. 30 o in inclination which suggested that the geomagnetic fietd source at the time that these lavas were erupted, may have been more complex than an axial geocentric dipole. The present study has aimed to investigate the significance of this reversal asymmetry by resolv- ing the detailed component structure in the lavas using thermal demagnetisation and modern tech- niques of component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980). This study also extends the section sampled by Piper (1977) to cover the entire 1500 m of lava stratigraphy, with the hope of identifying any further reversals in the previously unsampled up- per 200 m of the lava pile. It has also aimed to clarify the significance of anomalous results ob- tained by Piper, mainly in the middle of the three lava groups. 2. Geology and sampling The Gardar igneous province of South Green- land records an approximately 200 Ma period of persistent crustal movements and alkaline mag- matism. Between five and ten three-inch cores were drilled from each flow using a portable two-stroke motor and water-cooled diamond drill bit. The cores were oriented in situ, before re- moval from the outcrop, using a sun compass in conjunction with a magnetic compass. Four one- inch cores were cut from each site in the labora- tory, for palaeomagnetic measurements. 3. These temperatures are too low to have unblocked a TRM component possessing such a high blocking temperature (Pullaiah et al., 1975) over the likely duration (up to several millions of years) of the hydrothermal event. Moreover, there is no obvious reason why only the middle of the three groups should be remagnetised as a result of regional hydrothermal alteration, to produce a secondary chemical remanence (CRM). The high oxidation states of flows from the middle lavas (Piper, 1977) suggests that deuteric oxidation may be responsible for the haematite present. Piper (1977) attributed the anomalous direc- tion to either an apparent polar wander excursion or a transitional field direction. He favoured the former since the higher lavas in the middle group are separated by sandstones and their eruption must have scanned a considerable period of time. However, the new results question this interpre- tation. Figure 6a shows that a directional change occurs at the top of the middle lava group, with the change lost in the thin sediments between two flows. Crucially, the direction after the change is similar to the normal polarity (westerly) direc- tions witnessed in the upper and low

agnetostratigraphy documented here records the behaviour of the geomagnetic field over only a very short interval of geological time. During this short time, the field direction changed rapidly in the upper lava group, where no transitional directions are recog- nised, but remained locked in at a transitional direction for a longer period during the eruption of the middle lava group. This illustrates some analogies with the behaviour recognised in the Miocene Steens Mountain lavas (Prevot et al., 1985). Results from both this study and rock mag- netic studies of the Gardar lavas (Thomas, 1991) suggest that the existence of pure magnetite and haematite, and the absence of titanium-rich ti- tanomagnetites in the lavas may result from vari- ous stages of high temperature (deuteric) oxida- tion. Palaeointensity studies, “‘Ar:40Ar and U-Pb dating (B. Paterson, pers. commun., 1990) cur- rently in progress will constrain the cause and timing of the geomagnetic features documented here. agnetostratigraphy documented here records the behaviour of the geomagnetic field over only a very short interval of geological time. During this short time, the field direction changed rapidly in the upper lava group, where no transitional directions are recog- nised, but remained locked in at a transitional direction for a longer period during the eruption of the middle lava group. This illustrates some analogies with the behaviour recognised in the Miocene Steens Mountain lavas (Prevot et al., 1985). Results from both this study and rock mag- netic studies of the Gardar lavas (Thomas, 1991) suggest that the existence of pure magnetite and haematite, and the absence of titanium-rich ti- tanomagnetites in the lavas may result from vari- ous stages of high temperature (deuteric) oxida- tion. agnetostratigraphy documented here records the behaviour of the geomagnetic field over only a very short interval of geological time. During this short time, the field direction changed rapidly in the upper lava group, where no transitional directions are recog- nised, but remained locked in at a transitional direction for a longer period during the eruption of the middle lava group. This illustrates some analogies with the behaviour recognised in the Miocene Steens Mountain lavas (Prevot et al., 1985). Results from both this study and rock mag- netic studies of the Gardar lavas (Thomas, 1991) suggest that the existence of pure magnetite and haematite, and the absence of titanium-rich ti- tanomagnetites in the lavas may result from vari- ous stages of high temperature (deuteric) oxida- tion. agnetostratigraphy documented here records the behaviour of the geomagnetic field over only a very short interval of geological time. During this short time, the field direction changed rapidly in the upper lava group, where no transitional directions are recog- nised, but remained locked in at a transitional direction for a longer period during the eruption of the middle lava group. This illustrates some analogies with the behaviour recognised in the Miocene Steens Mountain lavas (Prevot et al., 1985). Results from both this study and rock mag- netic studies of the Gardar lavas (Thomas, 1991) suggest that the existence of pure magnetite and haematite, and the absence of titanium-rich ti- tanomagnetites in the lavas may result from vari- ous stages of high temperature (deuteric) oxida- tion. Palaeointensity studies, “‘Ar:40Ar and U-Pb dating (B. Paterson, pers. commun., 1990) cur- rently in progress will constrain the cause and timing of the geomagnetic features documented here. The two distributions can be matched by adjustment for ca. 95 km of sinistral strike slip on the site of the Minches Basin between the two outcrops. This fault zone is the NW member of a suite of NE-SW trending transcurrent faults active in late Caledonian times and possesses the largest strike-slip offset. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving structures referred to the Badcallian episode ~2800-2600 Ma) of relict granulite facies. It is bordered by broad zones to the north and south (the Northern and Southern Zones) comprehensively reworked during the Laxfordian episode (ca. 1900-1700 Ma) and retrogressed to amphiboI~te-facies. The earli- est members were emplaced into active late Scourian NW-SE shears, while later members are preserved as discordant dykes. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving struct

gs. 1 to 4) is a complex series of thrusts and crush zones extending along the full length of the eastern seaboard. Fettes and Mendum (1987) link its initiation at depths of lo-15 km to a compres- sional phase early in the post-Laxfordian uplift. Mylonites, pseudotachylites and cataclastic rocks are present within this zone (Sibson, 1975). Ow- ing to its proximity (ca. 90 km) to the Caledonian erogenic margin, it was reactivated again in Lower Palaeozoic times. Fault products of both post- Laxfordian and Palaeozoic age are identified by K-Ar (Rex and Moorbath in Sibson, 1975) and palaeomagnetic (Piper and Poppleton, 1988) data. The best that can be achieved is sampling within the contact aureoles of sparse Permo- Carboniferous and Tertiary dykes which cut the basement. However, palaeomagnetic studies of Lewisian clasts in conglomerates at the base of the Stoer (Piper and Poppleton, 1990) and Torri- don (Smith and Piper, 1982; Poppleton and Piper, 1989) Group sedimentary successions on the mainland show that Lewisian rocks are domi- nated by a remanence predating deposition of these successions at ca. 1100 and 1040 Ma respec- tively (Smith et al., 1983). Hence there is little doubt that the remanence in the basement of the Outer Hebrides was fixed between the time of the Laxfordian episode (when regional tempera- tures were in the range 700-500°C; see Dickin- son and Watson, 1976, and O’Hara, 1977) and the time of Torridonian sedimentation. Although isolated areas of granulite facies are preserved, (Dearnley, 19631, the bulk of the Outer Hebrides outcrop was retrogressed to amphibo- lite facies during waning stages of the Laxfordian episode. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving struct

Fettes and Mendum (1987) link its initiation at depths of lo-15 km to a compres- sional phase early in the post-Laxfordian uplift. Mylonites, pseudotachylites and cataclastic rocks are present within this zone (Sibson, 1975). Ow- ing to its proximity (ca. 90 km) to the Caledonian erogenic margin, it was reactivated again in Lower Palaeozoic times. patial distribution of magnetisations in the Outer Hebrides basement mirrors the distribution observed in the Mainland outcrop comprising the NW foreland to the Caledonian orogen but is displaced laterally. The two distributions can be matched by adjustment for ca. 95 km of sinistral strike slip on the site of the Minches Basin between the two outcrops. This fault zone is the NW member of a suite of NE-SW trending transcurrent faults active in late Caledonian times and possesses the largest strike-slip offset. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving structures referred to the Badcallian episode ~2800-2600 Ma) of relict granulite facies. It is bordered by broad zones to the north and south (the Northern and Southern Zones) comprehensively reworked during the Laxfordian episode (ca. 1900-1700 Ma) and retrogressed to amphiboI~te-facies. Subsequent deformation resulted in gneiss formation. Following emplacement of a suite of diorite intrusives, the complex was de- formed into NNE-SSW folds in late Scourian (26~0-2400 Ma) times. Division (b) comprises peridotite, picrite, norite and (most abundantly~ microdolerite dykes, sheets and lenses. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving struct

gs. 1 to 4) is a complex series of thrusts and crush zones extending along the full length of the eastern seaboard. Fettes and Mendum (1987) link its initiation at depths of lo-15 km to a compres- sional phase early in the post-Laxfordian uplift. Mylonites, pseudotachylites and cataclastic rocks are present within this zone (Sibson, 1975). Ow- ing to its proximity (ca. 90 km) to the Caledonian erogenic margin, it was reactivated again in Lower Palaeozoic times. Fault products of both post- Laxfordian and Palaeozoic age are identified by K-Ar (Rex and Moorbath in Sibson, 1975) and palaeomagnetic (Piper and Poppleton, 1988) data. However, palaeomagnetic studies of Lewisian clasts in conglomerates at the base of the Stoer (Piper and Poppleton, 1990) and Torri- don (Smith and Piper, 1982; Poppleton and Piper, 1989) Group sedimentary successions on the mainland show that Lewisian rocks are domi- nated by a remanence predating deposition of these successions at ca. 1100 and 1040 Ma respec- tively (Smith et al., 1983). Hence there is little doubt that the remanence in the basement of the Outer Hebrides was fixed between the time of the Laxfordian episode (when regional tempera- tures were in the range 700-500°C; see Dickin- son and Watson, 1976, and O’Hara, 1977) and the time of Torridonian sedimentation. Although isolated areas of granulite facies are preserved, (Dearnley, 19631, the bulk of the Outer Hebrides outcrop was retrogressed to amphibo- lite facies during waning stages of the Laxfordian episode. this episode (Fettes and Mendum, 1987). Division (a) is predominantly of igneous (tona- lite, granodiorite and anorthosite) parentage and derived at ca. 2900-2800 Ma from an upper man- tle source. patial distribution of magnetisations in the Outer Hebrides basement mirrors the distribution observed in the Mainland outcrop comprising the NW foreland to the Caledonian orogen but is displaced laterally. It appears to be controlled mainly by Laxfordian strain although the effect of the earlier Scourian episode is also recorded. A younger iamprophyr~ dyke suite yields a palaeomagnetic pole from nine sites (349” E. 47”s) dated as mid-Permian by reference to the Eurasian APW path. The spatial distribution of magnetisations in the Outer Hebrides basement mirrors the distribution observed in the Mainland outcrop comprising the NW foreland to the Caledonian orogen but is displaced laterally. The two distributions can be matched by adjustment for ca. 95 km of sinistral strike slip on the site of the Minches Basin between the two outcrops. This fault zone is the NW member of a suite of NE-SW trending transcurrent faults active in late Caledonian times and possesses the largest strike-slip offset. Introduction Metamorphic basement complexes possess magnetic remanence acquired during stow uplift- related cooling below the Curie point. This rema- nence postdates the last ductile phases of defor- mation and is a sensitive indicator of late events in the consolidation of these complexes such as uprising fluids during retrogressive metamor- phism. The Lewisian terrane of NW Scotland comprises a Central Zone preserving struct

gs. 1 to 4) is a complex series of thrusts and crush zones extending along the full length of the eastern seaboard. Fettes and Mendum (1987) link its initiation at depths of lo-15 km to a compres- sional phase early in the post-Laxfordian uplift. Mylonites, pseudotachylites and cataclastic rocks are present within this zone (Sibson, 1975). Ow- ing to its proximity (ca. 90 km) to the Caledonian erogenic margin, it was reactivated again in Lower Palaeozoic times. Fault products of both post- Laxfordian and Palaeozoic age are identified by K-Ar (Rex and Moorbath in Sibson, 1975) and palaeomagnetic (Piper and Poppleton, 1988) data. Granulite facies metamorphism takes place above the Curie point and may produce metamorphic magnetite during the prograde phase (Rumble, 1976). Amphibolite facies meta- morphism takes place close to, or below, the Curie point and the effects are more complex. A general effect of fluid accession associated with the higher grades of Laxfordian amphibolite fa- ties metamorphism is enhancement of the mag- netite content (Piper, 1992). In: H. Perroud and G. Bylund (Editors). Palaeomagnetism of Old European Rocks. Tectonophysics, 201: (spec. sect.): 83-96. Four different characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) orientations have been isolated in the El Adeb Larache formation of the Algerian Sahara (27.45”N. 8.9’EE). Two of them are interpreted as overprints developed respectively during recent and Permian times. The two others give new Moscovian (28.7 ’ S, 55.8 o El and probably Stephano-Autunian (38.5 OS, 57.5 o E) palaeopoles. in good agreement with those previously obtained from the Sahara, but significantly different from the Dwyka “vatves” pole (McElhinny and Opdyke, 1968). Comparison with Lower Carboniferous results shows that the latitudinal displacement of Africa during the Carboniferous is mainly related to a clockwise rotation (about 25 ’ ) around an axis close to the northeastern border of Africa. Such a motion of Africa agrees well with geological observations and with the Pangea A2 hypothesis. ica agrees well with geological observations and with the Pangea A2 hypothesis. Introduction Even if sound post-Jurassic palaeocontinental reconstructions have been obtained combining magnetic anomalies and palaeomagnetic data (Le Pichon and Fox, 1971; Pitman and Talwani, 1972; Olivet et al., 19841, evolution of the Pangea con- figuration from Carboniferous to Triassic is al- ways hypothetical. Based mainly on palaeomag- netic data, several different evolution models have been proposed (Irving, 1977; Van der Voo, 1981; Merabet, 1987). One of the major uncertainties for this period is that the African apparent polar wander path (APWP) is poorly constrained (see Bachtadse and Briden, 1989, 1990; Feinberg et al., 19901 due to large time gaps in the palaeo- magnetic data set as well as conflicting results for the same period (McElhinny and Opdyke, 1968; Daly and Irving, 1983). Such incoherence in the results may be related to several causes. Firstly, the fact that some natu- ral remanent magnetizations (NRM) are com- plete overprints, is not always easy to point out (see for example Triassic formations in Lybia and southern Tunisia-Nairn and Martin, 1978, and Ghorabi, 1990; the Gneiguira supergroup-Kent et al., 1984; or the Karoo basin-Ballard et al., 1986). S

ck of adequate demagnetiza- tion experiments in some studies may have masked possible multicomponent NRM’s. Finally, age determination of rocks studied was some- times doubtful. For reasons such as the last two mentioned, the Msissi norite results (Hailwood, 1974) can no longer be thought of as being repre- sentative of a Devonian palaeomagnetic pole (Salmon et al., 1987). Four different characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) orientations have been isolated in the El Adeb Larache formation of the Algerian Sahara (27.45”N. 8.9’EE). Two of them are interpreted as overprints developed respectively during recent and Permian times. The two others give new Moscovian (28.7 ’ S, 55.8 o El and probably Stephano-Autunian (38.5 OS, 57.5 o E) palaeopoles. in good agreement with those previously obtained from the Sahara, but significantly different from the Dwyka “vatves” pole (McElhinny and Opdyke, 1968). Comparison with Lower Carboniferous results shows that the latitudinal displacement of Africa during the Carboniferous is mainly related to a clockwise rotation (about 25 ’ ) around an axis close to the northeastern border of Africa. Based mainly on palaeomag- netic data, several different evolution models have been proposed (Irving, 1977; Van der Voo, 1981; Merabet, 1987). One of the major uncertainties for this period is that the African apparent polar wander path (APWP) is poorly constrained (see Bachtadse and Briden, 1989, 1990; Feinberg et al., 19901 due to large time gaps in the palaeo- magnetic data set as well as conflicting results for the same period (McElhinny and Opdyke, 1968; Daly and Irving, 1983). Palaeobiogeograpby Spjeldmes (1961) suggested that Ordovician fauna1 provinces correspond to distinct climatic zones, and later papers developed this idea to produce palaeogeographical reconstructions based on evidence from the study of sediments and benthic faunas. In these, the Baltic province has always been considered different from the Gondwana and North American provinces. This has been particularly well illustrated for trilobites (Whittington and Hughes, 1972) and brachiopods (Williams, 1973; Jaanusson, 1973; Neuman, 1984; Bruton and Harper, 1985). The isolation of these provinces is thought to be related to climatic zonation and to oceanic barriers, the Proto- Atlantic (Iapetus) Ocean and the mid-European Ocean separating them. Subsequent studies and more detailed analysis of the Ordovician sedi- mentary successions and faunas did not upset these reconstructions which have only been slightly modified, more fully illustrated, and more precisely delimited. At present there is a general consensus about the global palaeogeographic configuration for the Ordovician Period despite some discrepancies as those concern

It is therefore regarded as pa- rautochthonous (Bockelie and Nystuen, 1985). The Permian igneous activity was particularly im- portant in this area. The autochthonous Ordottieian in Norway and Sweden During the Ordovician, an epicontinental sea extended over the entire Baltic platform from west of the Oslo Region to the Moscow basin in the east (Bruton and Williams, 1982; Bruton, 1989). Most of the areas sampled are within the “Central Baltoscandian belt” of Jaanusson (1976, 1982a), where carbonate sediments predominate, and the ““Scanian confacies belt” characterized by terrigenous sediments. Sequences are thin and the total thickness generally does not exceed 150-200 m in Sweden, although this figure is more than doubled in some parts of the Oslo Region, Norway (Bruton and Owen, 1982; Bruton et al., 1985). However, the mechanism for its acquisi- tion can be either purely thermal (that is without any change in the rock mineralogy), purely chem- ical (without any increase of temperature) or thermo-chemical (mineralogical changes trig- gered by temperature increase). The GA1 indexes clearly reveal that temperatures up to 300 O C were reached in most Ordovician rocks of the area, so the purely chemical mechanism can be excluded. However, there is some evidence that mineralogical changes took piace in the rocks as exemplified by the demagnetization diagrams of Fig. 4. One of many problems and still an open question, is the knowl- edge of the precise position of Baltica (Bal- toscandia and East-European-Russian platform) during the early Palaeozoic. De- spite the continued generation of new data that have led to successive modifications of these re- constructions, a general agreement about the Palaeozoic evolution has yet to be reached (Scotese and McKerrow, 1990). One of many problems and still an open question, is the knowl- edge of the precise position of Baltica (Bal- toscandia and East-European-Russian platform) during the early Palaeozoic. This has never been preciseIy constrained, hence new data are of great interest (Torsvik et al., 1990, p. 38). The aim of the present paper is to present and discuss palaeomagnetic results obtained from Or- dovician limestones in Sweden and Norway and to show how these may help solve the problem of the position of Baltica. However, the Ordovician latitudinal position of Baltica cannot be defined precisely by fauna1 and sedimentary evidence. Some reconstructions have shown the Baltic continent at equatorial latitudes (Whittington and Hughes, 1972) during the entire Ordovician, whereas other authors are rather in- clined to propose a more temperate position (Spjeldnaes, 1961). De- spite the continued generation of new data that have led to successive modifications of these re- constructions, a general agreement about the Palaeozoic evolution has yet to be reached (Scotese and McKerrow, 1990). One of many problems and still an open question, is the knowl- edge of the precise position of Baltica (Bal- toscandia and East-European-Russian platform) during the early Palaeozoic. This has never been preciseIy constrained, hence new data are of great interest (Torsvik et al., 1990, p. 38). The aim of the present paper is to present and discuss palaeomagnetic results obtained from Or- dovician limestones in Sweden and Norway and to show how these may help solve the problem of the position of Baltica. However, the Ordovician latitudinal position of Baltica cannot be defined precisely by fauna1 and sedimentary evidence. Some reconstructions have shown the Baltic continent at equatorial latitudes (Whittington and Hughes, 1972) during the entire Ordovician, whereas other authors are rather in- clined to propose a more temperate position (Spjeldnaes, 1961). Introduction Northern Brittany is characterized by a Pre- cambrian basement, structured during the Cado- mian orogeny and moderately affected by the Hercynian orogeny. It is intruded by a farge num- ber of doleritic dikes, concentrated in three major swarms (St Malo, Fougeres and TrCgor). In the St Malo doleritic swarm, all dikes are oriented ap- proximately N-S. They have been previously the

arboniferous (330 r;t 10 Ma) palaeomag- netic pole for the Armorican Massif. A palaeo- magnetic study of the Tregor doleritic swarm was of great interest as (1) the dikes, unlike the N-S orientations of the St Malo and Fougeres swarms, are oriented approximately E-W, and (2) prelim- inary K-Ar measurements revealed two age clus- ters around 350 Ma and 440450 Ma, which suggests that there might have been two or more phases of dike emplacement. Furthermore, palaeomagnetic data for the interval Upper Or- dovician-Lower Carboniferous are not available for the Armorican Massif, whereas data from this age are essential to test the new APWP proposed by Van der Voo (1988) and Bachtadse and Briden (1990) for Gondwana, which depends heavily on 0040-1951/92/$05.00 0 1992 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. Introduction Geological evidence suggests that the Apen- nine mountain range consists of several faulted and thrust geological units. These units originally belonged to the various isopic zones of the Alpine geosyncline in the southern margin of the Meso- zoic Tethys (Consiglio Nazionale delle Richerche, 1981). In the northern and central Apennines the external zones, which now trend north-south, are found. Each of these zones consists of tectonos- tratigraphic units derived from the deformation of pre-existing palaeogeographic units and at- tained their present position following several tectonic phases during the Neogene. In the west, the Tuscan zone (emplaced in Late Oligocene- Early Eocene) was thrust over the Umbria- Marche zone by the end of the Miocene. Later (Messinian-Pliocene) Umbria-Marche was itself thrust over the Abruzzi-Latium sequence to the east. Introduction Geological evidence suggests that the Apen- nine mountain range consists of several faulted and thrust geological units. These units originally belonged to the various isopic zones of the Alpine geosyncline in the southern margin of the Meso- zoic Tethys (Consiglio Nazionale delle Richerche, 1981). In the northern and central Apennines the external zones, which now trend north-south, are found. Each of these zones consists of tectonos- tratigraphic units derived from the deformation of pre-existing palaeogeographic units and at- tained their present position following several tectonic phases during the Neogene. In the west, the Tuscan zone (emplaced in Late Oligocene- Early Eocene) was thrust over the Umbria- Marche zone by the end of the Miocene. Later (Messinian-Pliocene) Umbria-Marche was itself thrust over the Abruzzi-Latium sequence to the east. Important easterly displacements of the Abruzzi-Campania zone over terrigenous Miocene beds have also been demonstrated. The magnetic mineralogy of the samples was inferred by experiments on induced remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition and demagneti- zation. Selected specimens from each site were subjected to incremental magnetization at room temperature in fields up to 0.95 T. Most of the resulting IRM acquisition curves are dominated by the presence of a magnetic mineral which is saturated in relatively low fields (h < 0.15 T) and which, by analogy to studies of pelagic limestones (e.g., Lowrie and Heller, 19821, we interpret to be magnetite (upper diagram Fig. 3a). In order to verify this interpretation, and to help identify the other magnetic minerals whose presence is indi- cated on some IRM curves by contributions ac- quired in fields greater than 0.15 T, an inverse IRM was given to each specimen subjected to these studies, which was subsequently demagne- tized thermally in suitable steps up to 680°C. (The inverse IRM was composed of an IRM induced along the specimen’s --z axis in a 0.95 T field and a second IRM of the same polarity applied along the i-z axis in a 0.15 T field.) Fine-grained pig- mentary haematite also occurs as an alteration product of clasts and within the matrix of the sandstones. The presence of antiparallel components of magnetisation within individual sites and the in- creased grouping of the data (Table 1) following differing bedding corrections suggest that mag- netisation of the Purilactis Formation occurred relatively rapidly after deposition. This inference is also supported by the fact that the pole posi- tion for the formation differs significantly from that of the overlying Paciencia Group (see below). Thus, magnetisation of the Purilactis Formation took place prior to deposition of the Paciencia Group and is therefore pre-Oligocene and proba- bly Palaeocene in age. ordillera (Gxdillera de Domeyko) of northern Chile. Comparison of isolated components of magnetisation from the Late Cretaceous-Palaeocene Purilactis Formation and the unconformably overlying Gligo-Miocene Paciencia Group with reference poles for South America indicate that significant post-Palaeocene and post-Lower Miocene clockwise rotation has taken place. A structural study of the area has revealed the presence of a number of thrust sheets that were periodically active throughout the Cenozoic. Stratigraphic, structural and palaeomagnetic data indicate that thrust sheet movement took place following deposition of both the Purilactis Formation (?lower Eocene Incaic Orogenyl and the Paciencia Group (?lowest Miocene Peheunche Orogeny) and resulted in the folding, uplift and clockwise rotation of the two sequences. Differences in the amount of rotation between the two units reflect incremental movement of the thrust sheets, 12” of rotation took place prior to deposition of the Paciencia Group followed by 17” of post-Lower Miocene clockwise rotation. This model is in good agreement with previous Cretaceous and Palaeogene palaeomagnetic data, which indicate counterclockwise rotations north of the deflec- tion, clockwise south of it, and negligible rota- tions in the region of the deflection itself (Palmer et al., 1980; Heki et al., 1983, 1984, 1985a,b; Turner et al., 1984; Kono et al., 1985; McFadden et al., 1985, 1990; May and Butler, 1985; Beck et al., 1986; Tanaka et al., 1988; Hartley et al., 1988; Mitouard et al., 1990). In contrast with Isacks’ model, Beck (1987, 1988) has proposed that, similar to the North- American Cordillera, the palaeomagnetic results reflect in-situ block rotations in response to the oblique convergence of the Nazca plate towards 0040-1951/92/$05.00 0 1992 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. In this type of model, the blocks, which rotate individually around verti- cal axes, are localized in a zone of distributed shear characterized by major strike-slip faults parallel to the coast. The blocks themselves are limited by many strike-slip faults oblique with respect to the previous ones (Beck, 1980). It has been suggested that this model could account for the rotations which postdate the

account for the rotations which postdate the accretion of allochthonous blocks in southern Ecuador and northern Peru where such faults have been recog- nized (MCgard et al., 1987; Roperch et al., 1987; Mourier et al., 1988; Laj et al., 1989; Mitouard et al., 1990). In the Central Andes of Peru, on the contrary, one may question whether Beck’s model provides a realistic explanation for their tectonic evolution, because no major strike-slip faults ap- pear to disturb the regularity of the Cainozoic folds. In only two regions, the Cajamarca area in the northern Central Andes and the Cuzco area, the folded Pre-Cainozoic sedimentary formations are affected by minor deflections caused by the sinistral reactivation of east-west palaeofaults (MCgard, 1987; Mourier, 1988); but this limited amount of faulting does not appear to have the amplitude and the widespread character required for block rotations to be a reasonable explanation of the rotated palaeomagnetic directions. A palaeomagnetic study was carried out in the region of Lima (Peru), on 55 sites (564 cores) of middle Cretaceous to Late Miocene age, distributed along three northeast-southwest transverses which cross the Western Cordillera of the Central Andes. Over the entire studied area, the results consistently yield westerly declinations corresponding to post-creta- ceous and post-Eocene counterclockwise rotations with respect to stable South America, of 16” f 6” and 13.7” + 8.1”, respectively, when compared to the ill-defined reference poles of this continent. In its western part, it comprises outcrops of late Juras- sic to middle Cretaceous sedimentary formations, covered during Albian times by the pillow lavas, tuffs, volcaniclastic sediments and black marly- limestones of the thick Casma Group (Cobbing, 1985). Introduction The Carpathian Fold Belt forms the most im- portant and complex arcuate structure of the East European part of the Alpine chain. The problem of the origin of the observed curvatures is still unresolved. Paleomagnetic data may help to determine whether the curvatures in a given region are original or the result of an oroclinal bending, i.e. a tectonic deformation of an origi- nally straight belt. Lowrie and Hirt (1986) showed how the relationship between the declination de- viation and fold axis deviation helps to resolve such problems in arcuate mountain belts. A simi- lar analysis was conducted by Bazhenov and Burtman (1990) for the Cretaceous rocks of the whole Carpathian Belt from the Southern Alps to the Eastern Pontides. Introduction The Carpathian Fold Belt forms the most im- portant and complex arcuate structure of the East European part of the Alpine chain. The problem of the origin of the observed curvatures is still unresolved. Paleomagnetic data may help to determine whether the curvatures in a given region are original or the result of an oroclinal bending, i.e. a tectonic deformation of an origi- nally straight belt. Lowrie and Hirt (1986) showed how the relationship between the declination de- viation and fold axis deviation helps to resolve such problems in arcuate mountain belts. A simi- lar analysis was conducted by Bazhenov and Burtman (1990) for the Cretaceous rocks of the whole Carpathian Belt from the Southern Alps to the Eastern Pontides. Their results suggest an oroclinal bending of originally parallel straight belts. The present paper reports the results of a Correspondence to: M. cinity of the Certovica Line in the Low Tatras (Bely and Fusan, 1967). During the Mediterranean phase of the Alpine orogeny these sediments were detached from their base- ment, pushed northward and folded. As a result of tectonic processes they were divided into three nappes lying one upon the other. The lowermost and best preserved Kriina Nappe lies directly on the Hightatric substratum, and its structure is probably closely related to the structure of the substratum rocks. The northward pushing and folding of the nappe resulted in its fragmentation into several separate nappe fragments. The KriZna Nappe sediments comprise rock formations from the Permian Verrucano (rarely exposed), through the Triassic and the Jurassic, up to the Lower Cretaceous. Introduction The Carpathian Fold Belt forms the most im- portant and complex arcuate structure of the East European part of the Alpine chain. The problem of the origin of the observed curvatures is still unresolved. Paleomagnetic data may help to determine whether the curvatures in a given region are original or the result of an oroclinal bending, i.e. a tectonic deformation of an origi- nally straight belt. During the Mediterranean phase of the Alpine orogeny these sediments were detached from their base- ment, pushed northward and folded. As a result of tectonic processes they were divided into three nappes lying one upon the other. The lowermost and best preserved Kriina Nappe lies directly on the Hightatric substratum, and its structure is probably closely related to the structure of the substratum rocks. The northward pushing and folding of the nappe resulted in its fragmentation into several separate nappe fragments. Introduction The Carpathian Fold Belt forms the most im- portant and complex arcuate structure of the East European part of the Alpine chain. The problem of the origin of the observed curvatures is still unresolved. Paleomagnetic data may help to determine whether the curvatures in a given region are original or the result of an oroclinal bending, i.e. a tectonic deformation of an origi- nally straight belt. Lowrie and Hirt (1986) showed how the relationship between the declination de- viation and fold axis deviation helps to resolve such problems in arcuate mountain belts. A simi- lar analysis was conducted by Bazhenov and Burtman (1990) for the Cretaceous rocks of the whole Carpathian Belt from the Southern Alps to the Eastern Pontides. Their results suggest an oroclinal bending of originally parallel straight belts. The present paper reports the results of a Correspondence to: M. cinity of the Certovica Line in the Low Tatras (Bely and Fusan, 1967). During the Mediterranean phase of the Alpine orogeny these sediments were detached from their base- ment, pushed northward and folded. As a result of tectonic processes they were divided into three nappes lying one upon the other. The lowermost and best preserved Kriina Nappe lies directly on the Hightatric substratum, and its structure is probably closely related to the structure of the substratum rocks. The northward pushing and folding of the nappe resulted in its fragmentation into several separate nappe fragments. The KriZna Nappe sediments comprise rock formations from the Permian Verrucano (rarely exposed), through the Triassic and the Jurassic, up to the Lower Cretaceous. Introduction The Carpathian Fold Belt forms the most im- portant and complex arcuate structure of the East European part of the Alpine chain. The problem of the origin of the observed curvatures is still unresolved. Paleomagnetic data may help to determine whether the curvatures in a given region are original or the result of an oroclinal bending, i.e. a tectonic deformation of an origi- nally straight belt. Lowrie and Hirt (1986) showed how the relationship between the declination de- viation and fold axis deviation helps to resolve such problems in arcuate mountain belts. A simi- lar analysis was conducted by Bazhenov and Burtman (1990) for the Cretaceous rocks of the whole Carpathian Belt from the Southern Alps to the Eastern Pontides. Their results suggest an oroclinal bending of originally parallel straight belts. The present paper reports the results of a Correspondence to: M. Kadzialko-Hofmokl, Institute of Geo- physics, Polish Academy of Science, ul. KS. Janusza 64,01-452 Warsaw, Poland. pa

cinity of the Certovica Line in the Low Tatras (Bely and Fusan, 1967). During the Mediterranean phase of the Alpine orogeny these sediments were detached from their base- ment, pushed northward and folded. As a result of tectonic processes they were divided into three nappes lying one upon the other. The lowermost and best preserved Kriina Nappe lies directly on the Hightatric substratum, and its structure is probably closely related to the structure of the substratum rocks. The northward pushing and folding of the nappe resulted in its fragmentation into several separate nappe fragments. The KriZna Nappe sediments comprise rock formations from the Permian Verrucano (rarely exposed), through the Triassic and the Jurassic, up to the Lower Cretaceous. Upper Cretaceous pelagic limestones exist in a few localities which escaped erosion. Paleocene emersion then eroded the Upper Cretaceous part of the Mesozoic cover. Further erosion is evidenced by Eocene marine conglomerates which contain pebbles of Lower, Middle, and Upper Jurassic limestones [Hollister, 1934; Bourrouilh, 1973; Stoeckinger, 1976a,b]. The Jurassic rocks may have acquired their ChRM during this emersion from Paleocene to lower Eocene. At present we have neither enough data nor an unambiguous fold test to determine if the ChRM is Jurassic and carried by magnetite or remagnetized and carried by fine- grained, secondary hematite with an early Tertiary remagnetization age. Secondary magnetization in an (unknown) uplifted and slightly tilted position could also explain the scatter which does not significantly improve with tectonic correction. For the conclusions presented in this paper it is not critical if magnetization occurred in the Jurassic or Early Tertiary. The available geologic and paleomagnetic data indicate that if remagnetization occurred, then it took place prior to Oligocene-Miocene folding and thrusting and most probably in the Paleocene. Over 400 rock samples from 30 sites were collected for paleomagnetic study from the volcanogenic section in the Brook Street termne within the Takitimu Mountains in western Southland, New Zealand. The section is divided into two distinct groups: the stratified Early Permian Takitimu Group and the Permian White Hill Intrusive Suite [Houghton, 1981, 1986]. Both groups are considered -part of the larger Brook Street tectonostratigraphic terrane. No continental detritus is found in the section, which suggests an oceanic origin. This conclusion is further supported by neodymium isotope data [Frost and Coorobs, 1987] which show oceanic values. EXPERIMENTAL PROCEDURE Over 400 samples from 30 sites were collected from the Takitimu Group and from the White Hill Intrusive Suite (Figure 2). In this study a site is defined as a set of samples taken from a single cooling unit or sedimentary horizon. Stmctmal attitudes were taken from interbedded sedimen units when possible. In areas where no structural attitude was available a regional attitude taken from maps of Houghton [1981] was used. Each sample was individually stepwise demagnetized using either stepwise alternating field (AF), stepwise thermal, or continuous thermal demagnetization [Dunn and Fuller, 1984]. Stable directions were selected using equal-area and Zijderveld [1967] vector end point plots coupled with the statistical methods of Kirschvink [1980]. Site averages were then computed using Fisher [1953] statistics. The oldest previously published pole from New Zealand is a Late Triassic/F. arly Jurassic result from the Murihiku terrane [Grindley et al., 1980]. The lack of older poles and a New Zealand apparent polar wander (APW) path make it impossible to test whether the Brook Street terrane is allochthonous. However, an APW path for Gondwana from Thompson and Clark [1982] was transferred (using rotation poles from Lawvex and Scotese [1987]) to New Zealand (Figure 7). Coombs DeImrUnent of Geology, University of Otago Dunedin, New Zealand Abstract. Over 400 rock samples from 30 sites were collected for paleomagnetic study from the volcanogenic section in the Brook Street termne within the Takitimu Mountains in western Southland, New Zealand. The section includes igneous and sedimentary rocks of the Permian Takitimu Group and White Hill Intrusive Suite. Many of the samples show a partial or complete remagnetization in the present field because of a recent acquisition of viscous remanent magnetization. An Early Permian direction (inclination = 46.1ø, declination = 257ø), isolated from the Heartbreak and Chimney Peaks formations of the Takitimu Group, indicates a low paleolatitude to midpaleolatitude, position (27 ø + 5 ø) for the Brook Street terrane. The section is divided into two distinct groups: the stratified Early Permian Takitimu Group and the Permian White Hill Intrusive Suite [Houghton, 1981, 1986]. Both groups are considered -part of the larger Brook Street tectonostratigraphic terrane. The Takitimu Group comprises a thick sequence of volcanic and volcaniclastic rocks, dominated by volcaniclastic sediments, deposited in an active island arc-related basin [Houghton, 1981]. No continental detritus is found in the section, which suggests an oceanic origin. This conclusion is further supported by neodymium isotope data [Frost and Coorobs, 1987] which show oceanic values. A paleomagnetic study of Devonian sedimentary sequences from western and eastern Yunnan, China, yields contrasting paleolatitudes for these two areas. They indicate an equatorial position for eastern Yunnan, as part of the Yangtze Paraplatform or South China Block, and a paleolatitude of about 40 ø for western Yunnan as part of the Shan State (or Shan-Thai) Block, which probably was part of the Gondwana supercontinent. The majority of samples is strongly overprinted by a present-day field magnetization, but thermal demagnetization has been successful in isolating ancient, dual- polarity characteristic directions of magnetization in rocks from eastern and western Yunnan, with results from the latter passing the fold test. The paleopole from eastern Yunnan is located at 8.9øN, 10.4øE (declination/inclination = 279.2ø/ +2.7 ø, k = 13, alpha 95 = 6.9 ø, N = 33 samples from 7 sites). A paleomagnetic study of Devonian sedimentary sequences from western and eastern Yunnan, China, yields contrasting paleolatitudes for these two areas. CCW declination deflections found in Mesozoic and Cenozoic rocks as far as 400 km east and 150 km south of Sarawak, in Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo), also fit the trend of deflection versus age. On the basis of the regional consistency of declination deflection versus age, along with geologic evidence the data are considered to be evidence of a regional (rather than a local block or distributed shear) rotation. The site mean directions are only slightly better clustered after correction, thus it is impossible to say whether the observed magnetization is predeformational (Table 2 and Figure 6). Folding of the formation probably occurred in the Miocene, but control on the age of deformation is poor [Tan, 1979]. Whether or not the magnetizations are predeformational, the anomalous sites are in good agreement and the means display an average of 38 ø CCW deflection prior to tectonic correction or 41 ø after. Haile [1979] reported paleomagnetic results from a site in the Silantek redbeds (Figures 4 and 6). The site mean is identical to the reverse equivalent of the present field vector. It is possible that the site comes from the youngest (Miocene?) part of the formation and is undetected. Remagnetization due to weathering in the tropical climate is a phenomenon we have commonly observed in other redbeds from Malaysia, and it is also possible that the site was recently remagnetized. The locations of those which yielded useable results are shown in Figure 4. In addition, N. S. Haile (personal communication, 1986) provided us with unpublished results from two stocks. It was impossible to determine paleohorizontal from nearby strata, but of the intrusions we sampled many display vertical columnar jointing, suggesting that tilting was probably small. Nine of 14 sites have stable magnetizations (Table 1 and Figure 5). The samples yield the same characteristic stable directions using either AFD or STD. Single component magnetization is predominant, and stable end points are easily selected. The 11 site mean directions are of both polarities. Site SR85-3 has an unexplained, anomalous direction, also found by N. S. Haile (personal communication, 1986). Four of the remaining 10 means show no declination deflection. The other six display significant counterclockwise (CCW) deflections. Five of these six sites have deflections of 8 ø to 26 ø , and the fifth is deflected 51.8 ø (Table 1). None of the 10 site mean declinations are significantly deflected CW. Prefolding directions, showing 90 ø of CCW deflection, are isolated in 4 sites (including two positive fold tests) in Upper Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks of the Bau Limestone and Pedawan Formations. CCW declination deflections found in Mesozoic and Cenozoic rocks as far as 400 km east and 150 km south of Sarawak, in Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo), also fit the trend of deflection versus age. On the basis of the regional consistency of declination deflection versus age, along with geologic evidence the data are considered to be evidence of a regional (rather than a local block or distributed shear) rotation. The domain of CCW rotation extends into West Malaysia, suggesting that West Borneo and the Malay Peninsula may have been a stable block during the latest Cretaceous and Cenozoic. W

Van Bemmelen [ 1949] assigned both exposures to the \"Natuna structural zone.\" Hamilton [1979] considered the rocks part of an arcuate, south dipping subduction complex, which extended northeast along offshore Vietnam and farther east in Sarawak. Shallow marine, marginal basin sediments were deposited across the Northwest Kalimantan domain in Upper Jurassic and Cretaceous time. Near-shore facies clastics and shallow marine limestones grade laterally and upward into basin fill sediments as much as 5 km thick [Wilford and Kho, 1965; Wolfenden, 1965; Muller, 1968; Williams et al., 1988] (Figures 2 and 3). These rocks are open to tightly folded about gently to moderately plunging, approximately east-west axes. Most of this deformation took place prior to the latest Cretaceous, since the rocks are unconformably overlain by the gently deformed, fluviatile Plateau Sandstone Formation, the basal part of which contains Senonian pollen (Figures 3 and 4) [Wilford and Kho, 1965; Muller, 1968; Williams et al., 1988]. Near-shore facies clastics and shallow marine limestones grade laterally and upward into basin fill sediments as much as 5 km thick [Wilford and Kho, 1965; Wolfenden, 1965; Muller, 1968; Williams et al., 1988] (Figures 2 and 3). Prior to 1940, Dutch geologists mapped extensively in Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo) [van Bemmelen, 1949]. Sarawak lies in both domains 1 and 3 (Figure 2). For clarity of discussion, and because their interpretation is the most recent, we follow their domain scheme. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: IC DATA FROM TERTIARY ROCKS Tertiary Intrusions We collected samples from 14 small stocks in West Sarawak. The locations of those which yielded useable results are shown in Figure 4. In addition, N. S. Haile (personal communication, 1986) provided us with unpublished results from two stocks. It was impossible to determine paleohorizontal from nearby strata, but of the intrusions we sampled many display vertical columnar jointing, suggesting that tilting was probably small. Nine of 14 sites have stable magnetizations (Table 1 and Figure 5). The samples yield the same characteristic stable directions using either AFD or STD. Prefolding directions, showing 90 ø of CCW deflection, are isolated in 4 sites (including two positive fold tests) in Upper Jurassic and Cretaceous rocks of the Bau Limestone and Pedawan Formations. CCW declination deflections found in Mesozoic and Cenozoic rocks as far as 400 km east and 150 km south of Sarawak, in Kalimantan (Indonesian Borneo), also fit the trend of deflection versus age. On the basis of the regional consistency of declination deflection versus age, along with geologic evidence the data are considered to be evidence of a regional (rather than a local block or distributed shear) rotation. The domain of CCW rotation extends into West Malaysia, suggesting that West Borneo and the Malay Peninsula may have been a stable block during the latest Cretaceous and Cenozoic. W

Middle to Late Jurassic sam- ples have been collected from granitic rocks in three geological subdivisions of South Korea, from north to south: Kyonggi Massif, Okchon Folded Belt and Ryongnam Massif. Triassic samples (granites and sediments) were collected in the Ryongnam Massif and its border area with the Okchon Folded Belt. The Jurassic declinations of the two massifs are northeasterly (mean D/I = 39.60/+57.6 ø , N = 7 sites, k = 31, e95 = 11.1 ø) , whereas the intervening Okchon Folded Belt reveals northwesterly Jurassic declinations (D/I = 337.5 ø/+47 ø , N = 7 sites, k = 32, e95 = 10.8 ø) . Reversed-polarity directions are rare, but have been observed in three localities. This oroge- nic belt, deformed in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous Daebo Orogeny, contains questionable ophiolites of pre-Jurassic(?) age, which has led some authors to suggest that it is a pre-Cretaceous suture [e.g., Lee, 1987, p. 225] . In order to test some of these ideas about Korean geologic subdivisions, as well as the paleogeographic setting of Korea in comparison with the China Blocks and Eurasia, Jurassic and Triassic granites and sediments were sampled for a paleomagnetic study. The Kyonggi Massif is separated from the North Korean Pyongnam Basin by the Chugaryong (also Shugareong) Zone or suture [e.g., Lee et al., 1987] , although this lineament is not mentioned as a suture by Lee [1987] and at any rate is likely to be of Paleozoic age [Lee et al., 1987]. Middle to Late Jurassic sam- ples have been collected from granitic rocks in three geological subdivisions of South Korea, from north to south: Kyonggi Massif, Okchon Folded Belt and Ryongnam Massif. Triassic samples (granites and sediments) were collected in the Ryongnam Massif and its border area with the Okchon Folded Belt. The Jurassic declinations of the two massifs are northeasterly (mean D/I = 39.60/+57.6 ø , N = 7 sites, k = 31, e95 = 11.1 ø) , whereas the intervening Okchon Folded Belt reveals northwesterly Jurassic declinations (D/I = 337.5 ø/+47 ø , N = 7 sites, k = 32, e95 = 10.8 ø) . This oroge- nic belt, deformed in the Late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous Daebo Orogeny, contains questionable ophiolites of pre-Jurassic(?) age, which has led some authors to suggest that it is a pre-Cretaceous suture [e.g., Lee, 1987, p. 225] . In order to test some of these ideas about Korean geologic subdivisions, as well as the paleogeographic setting of Korea in comparison with the China Blocks and Eurasia, Jurassic and Triassic granites and sediments were sampled for a paleomagnetic study. The Kyonggi Massif is separated from the North Korean Pyongnam Basin by the Chugaryong (also Shugareong) Zone or suture [e.g., Lee et al., 1987] , although this lineament is not mentioned as a suture by Lee [1987] and at any rate is likely to be of Paleozoic age [Lee et al., 1987]. tion. The Okchon Folded Belt (also spelled Ogcheon) separates the Kyonggi Massif to the north from the Ryongnam Massif to the south, as it runs diagonally across the Korean Peninsula (Figure 2). Magnetization was measured in most cases on a two-axis SCT cryogenic magnetometer; where intensities exceeded the range of this device, a Digico spinner magnetometer was used. These latter consist predominantly of blue-grey calcisiltites and calcilutites, the colour rapidly altering to cream upon drying. The calcisiltites are soft and highly porous. They are often well bedded. More active environmental conditions are indicated by frequent calcarenites and pebbly mudstones. Brown mudstone bands up to a few centimeters in width occur in places; the thin, turbiditic mudstone bands of the Haruta section are far less common in the Hada Calcisiltites. The basement of the Central Province includes at least 2000 m of pre-late Eocene (?) mafic lavas and gabbro and diabase intrusions; unlike the Pacific Province these have been subjected to extensive metamorphism of low to intermediate grade (greenschist and amphibolite facies). This metamorphism, occurring during the late Eocene to early Oligocene and accompanied by an unconformity in sedimentation, may mark the initiation of subduction along the north-eastern margin of the arc [Coulson and Vedder, 1986]. Gabbroic and ultramafic material was intruded in the late Cretaceous to early Tertiary. Late Oligocene to Holocene limestones, calcarenites, turbidites and volcaniclastics form an unconformable cover with a maximum thickness of about 5000 m developed in Guadalcanal. Intermediate to acid volcanics and intrusives of late Oligocene to early Miocene and late Miocene to Pleistocene age also occur [Pound, 1986]. The Volcanic Province comprises the presently active arc. It is centered on the New Georgia Group and is characterized by Pliocene to Holocene basaltic and andesitic cones and their surrounding epiclastic apron. The boundary between the Volcanic and Central Provinces is gradational, but the on-land boundary between the Central and Pacific Provinces ha

The Volcanic Province comprises the presently active arc. It is centered on the New Georgia Group and is characterized by Pliocene to Holocene basaltic and andesitic cones and their surrounding epiclastic apron. The boundary between the Volcanic and Central Provinces is gradational, but the on-land boundary between the Central and Pacific Provinces has been chosen to coincide with the Kia-Korigole-Kaipito (KKK) fault system in Santa Isabel [Coleman and Hackman, 1974]. The implication that the Pacific Province may be fault bounded along its entire southern margin is consistent with a view of the Central and Pacific Provinces as formerly distinct tectonostratigraphic terranes. INTRODUCTION Rocks of the deep crust, whether of metamorphic or plutonic origin, acquire a magnetization in the direction of the geomagnetic field (paleodirection) as they are uplifted and cooled [Pullaiah et al., 1975]. Such \"uplift\" magnetizations are amongst the simplest forms of remanent magnetization. They have been extensively observed in Precambrian rocks, especially in the Grenville Province of eastern Canada [Berger et al., 1979; Irving et al., 1974]. For rocks containing fine-grained magnetite, 580'C is the critical magnetic blocking temperature, although if cooling is slow, the blocking temperature may be lowered, but not by more than about 20'C [York, 1978]. If uplift is rapid, say 1 mm yr4, then a crustal layer 10 km thick would acquire an essentially uniform paleodirection, because significant apparent polar wander rarely occurs in an interval as short as 10 Ma. Tilting following uplift and cooling would be recorded as aberrant paleodirections, which can be used to estimate the attitude of the paleohorizontal plane just prior to uplift. Paleomagnetism has long been used in this general fashion as a means of estimating tilt in rocks of deep- seated origin [e.g. Hood,

ed. This implies that tilts of the magnitude encountered in supracrustal sequences of extensional zones extend also to deep-seated plutons and metamorphic rocks of the middle crust. The purpose of our study was to determine if such tilts occurred more generally in the extensional zone of southeast British Columbia, and particularly if they occurred symmetrically about the central culmination of this zone of extension. This paper presents results of paleomagnetic analysis of 10 localities, comprising 137 sites (1026 samples), in middle Eocene Challis volcanic rocks. Orientations were taken with magnetic and when possible with sun compass (only three sites because of rather un- friendly weather). Bedding directions were taken at three to twelve places at each site, being careful to avoid cross bedding which was observed at all scales up to tens of meters. Most samples were demagnetized themally, as alternating field demagnetization never efficiently isolated magnetic components. At least 10 demagnetization steps were done on each sample. Samples were measured in Paris with a C'IF three-axis cryogenic magnetometer and in Beijing with a Sch6nstedt fluxgate spinner. Directions and great-circle demagnetization paths were isolated using principal com- ponent analysis [Kirschvink, 1980], and site averages were found with McFadden and McElhinny's [1988] method. The relationship between the remanent magnetization and the detailed strain geometry around a first-order fold in the Appalachian Valley and Ridge Province was investigated to examine whether penetrative strains associated with folding can generate a apparent synfolding geometry from a prefolding magnetization. Paleomagnetic results from the Mississippian Mauch Chunk Formation on both limbs of the Frackville Anticline near Lavelle, Pennsylvania, yield two magnetic components, an intermediate unblocking temperature (300oc-600oc) Kiaman remagnetization and a two-polarity high unblocking temperature (650oc-680oc) characteristic magnetization. When the magnetic directions are incrementally corrected for bedding tilt, the intermediate-temperature component is most tightly clustered at 85% unfolding (D = 176 o, I = 3 o) and the high-temperature component is most tightly clustered at 75% unfolding (D = 184 o, I = 270). Mesoscopic and microscopic structural fabric analyses suggest a strain history that includes a significant component of flexural slip/flow folding. For rigid particle behavior the basal plane will rotate in the same sense as the shear. CONCLUSIONS Structural analysis in the Mauch Chunk Formation exposed on both limbs of the Frackville Anticline indicates a progressive deformation history that includes a significant component of bedding-parallel shear associated with folding. Finite strain measurements yield strain ellipsoids consistent with flexural flow and suggest that this stage in the deformation sequence has rotated the preexisting fabric e

These rotations result in shallower remanent inclinations on the south dipping limb, steeper remanent inclinations on the north dipping limb, and a apparent synfolding geometry from a prefolding magnetization. The sense of this rotation also suggests that the larger hematite grains, which carry the C component, behave as rigid particles not passive markers during deformation. Unlike the characteristic magnetization, the B component remanence, which is carded by the smaller pigmentary hematite flakes, appears to be unaffected by the deformation. c experiments suggest that the mechanism for remagnetization was through the formation of fine-grained magnetite and hematite and was probably controlled by local variation in fluid migration. The mean in situ direction for the 12 sites is I = -70.2% D=14.4 ø (a95=7.1 ø, kappa=38.6), which is significantly different from the predicted axial dipole field directions at the 95% confidence level. The age of the remagnetization is unclear. In an effort to date the remagnetization, a synthetic apparent polar wander (APW) path was constructed for New Zealand using Australian data, and the apparent south pole from the remagnetized Waipapa sites (latitude=69.7øS, longitude=150.7øE, a95=11.2 ø) was compared to this APW path. Using this method, the age of the remagnetization is constrained to be between --12 and 58 Ma. A major change in the tectonic regime occurred at --25 Ma, which is evidenced by obduction of the Northland allochthon and initiation of arc volcanism and subduction. Fluid migration and/or elevated temperatures driven by the initiation of subduction and arc volcanism, along with the obduction of the Northland allochthon seem likely mechanisms for the remagnetization. 975] referred to the upper plate as the Sapphire tectonic block, a Late Cretaceous feature. We refer to a similar crustal domain, of greater regional extent and Tertiary in age, as the Skalkaho slab. The Bitterroot mylonite's kinematics show that the Skalkaho slab/Sapphire tectonic block once overlay the Bitterroot dome. However, the timing and tectonics of the separation are equivocal. Hyndman et al. [1975] and Hyndman [ 1980] proposed that the Sapphire tectonic block slid to the east during the Late Cretaceous. Yet, Chase et al. [1983] and Garmezy [1983] suggest that the Bitterroot dome was pulled westward during the Eocene. A dike swarm of middle Eocene age (Figure lb) intrudes the Bitterroot dome and the Skalkaho slab. The average strike of the dike swarm is N21øE in the Bitterroot dome and N47øE in the Skalkaho slab. The divergent strikes imply that either (1) the Bitterroot dome and/or the Skalkaho slab moved since emplacement or (2) the dikes intruded in a refracted stress system. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a paleomagnetic study of the dikes. Our results indicate the Skalkaho slab rotated after emplacement of the dikes. 975] referred to the upper plate as the Sapphire tectonic block, a Late Cretaceous feature. We refer to a similar crustal domain, of greater regional extent and Tertiary in age, as the Skalkaho slab. The Bitterroot mylonite's kinematics show that the Skalkaho slab/Sapphire tectonic block once overlay the Bitterroot dome. However, the timing and tectonics of the separation are equivocal. Hyndman et al. [1975] and Hyndman [ 1980] proposed that the Sapphire tectonic block slid to the east during the Late Cretaceous. Yet, Chase et al. [1983] and Garmezy [1983] suggest that the Bitterroot dome was pulled westward during the Eocene. A dike swarm of middle Eocene age (Figure lb) intrudes the Bitterroot dome and the Skalkaho slab. The average strike of the dike swarm is N21øE in the Bitterroot dome and N47øE in the Skalkaho slab. The divergent strikes imply that either (1) the Bitterroot dome and/or the Skalkaho slab moved since emplacement or (2) the dikes intruded in a refracted stress system. To test these hypotheses, we conducted a paleomagnetic study of the dikes. Our results indicate the Skalkaho slab rotated after emplacement of the dikes. The oldest major unit, Mackenzie Moun- tains Supergroup (see Jefferson and Parrish, 1989 for history of definition) is a platformal sequence of carbonate, evaporite, and gener- ally mature terrigenous detrital strata (Aitken, 1982) which were deposited under warm cli- matic conditions. It is capped by the Lit- tle Dal basalts which are undated but chemi- cally similar to the diabase (ibid.). Several alternative apparent polar wander (APW) paths have been constructed using pri- mary and secondary magnetic components (Morris, 1977; Park, 1981a; Morris and Park, 1981; Park and Aitken, 1986a, b). Primary poles from the Mackenzie Mountains Super- group form a reasonably consistent APW path that could join the older Grenville Loop near the Equator in the Pacific Ocean (Park and Aitken, 1986a), but most secondary poles are not easy to relate to this path. One specific problem is whether poles, which indicate high paleolatitudes and are derived from hematite pigment in glaciogenic strata, are Late Pre- cambrian or Cretaceous in age. This study was initiated to test the signifi- cance of the Coates Lake Group's basal uncon- formity, which was documented stratigraphi- cally by Aitken ( 1981 ), paleomagnetically by Morris and Aitken (1982), and further de- scribed by Jefferson and Parrish (1989). Re- suits from this study also provide constraints on the nature of rifting, high-latitude poles, and the relative ages of hematite pigments. These results also help to interpret other unconform- ities such as that between the Redstone River and Thundercloud formations of Coates Lake Group,

Magnetic and tectonic history of the Late Proterozoic Upper Little Dal and Coates Lake groups of northwestern Canada. Precambrian Res., 52: 1-35. A pre- to syn-rift sequence (upper Little Dal Group, Coates Lake Group) in the Mackenzie Mountains of northwestern Canada reveals paleomagnetic directions in pigmental hematite (THs, RRa) that are similar to hematite overprint direc- tions (P2) of underlying Late Proterozoic strata. Paleopoles of these magnetic components from the Thundercloud and overlying Redstone River formations of the Coates Lake Group are respectively 202 ° W, 27 °N (N= 6 sites, A95 = 9 ° ) and 206°W, 32°N (N=4 sites, A95= 10 ° ). The primary paleopole for the basal Thundercloud Formation (THA) at 210°W, 01 °N (N=6 sites, A9s=21 ° ) is close to a previously reported pole (222°W, 2°N) from diabases (dated by U-Pb at 778 + 2 Ma) that intrude strata below Little Dal Group. The large error in THA, caused by scatter along a small circle, is here attributed mainly to tectonic rotation of azimuths of section-mean directions. Based on this interpretation, the

ections in magnetic phases of the Redstone River Formation are also interpreted to record local block rota- tions during trans-tensional tectonism. The P2 disseminated pigmemal hematite magnetization is interpreted to immediately postdate magnetizations from most other hematite phases, as well as magnetizations from (reduced) sulphide/magnetite beds at the base of the Copper- cap Formation (upper Coates Lake Group). P2 is absent from, and likely predates deposition of, the upper Coppercap and overlying formations. Some poles (P3) that postdate P2 poles and indicate high paleolatitudes are here interpreted as Late Precambrian. Negative fold tests suggest that most other high-latitude poles from Late Proterozoic units of the region are of Cretaceous Laramide age. Magnetic and tectonic history of the Late Proterozoic Upper Little Dal and Coates Lake groups of northwestern Canada. Precambrian Res., 52: 1-35. A pre- to syn-rift sequence (upper Little Dal Group, Coates Lake Group) in the Mackenzie Mountains of northwestern Canada reveals paleomagnetic directions in pigmental hematite (THs, RRa) that are similar to hematite overprint direc- tions (P2) of underlying Late Proterozoic strata. Paleopoles of these magnetic components from the Thundercloud and overlying Redstone River formations of the Coates Lake Group are respectively 202 ° W, 27 °N (N= 6 sites, A95 = 9 ° ) and 206°W, 32°N (N=4 sites, A95= 10 ° ). The primary paleopole for the basal Thundercloud Formation (THA) at 210°W, 01 °N (N=6 sites, A9s=21 ° ) is close to a previously reported pole (222°W, 2°N) from diabases (dated by U-Pb at 778 + 2 Ma) that intrude strata below Little Dal Group. The large error in THA, caused by scatter along a small circle, is

n THA, caused by scatter along a small circle, is here attributed mainly to tectonic rotation of azimuths of section-mean directions. Based on this interpretation, the THA pole position suggests a minimal unconformity below the Thundercloud Formation, contemporaneity of the sills and the basalts that cap the Little Dal Group, and uncom- formity between Thundercloud and Redstone River Formations. Anomalous directions from the Little Dal basalts, and sequential directions in magnetic phases of the Redstone River Formation are also interpreted to record local block rota- tions during trans-tensional tectonism. The P2 disseminated pigmemal hematite magnetization is interpreted to immediately postdate magnetizations from most other hematite phases, as well as magnetizations from (reduced) sulphide/magnetite beds at the base of the Copper- cap Formation (upper Coates Lake Group). P2 is absent from, and likely predates deposition of, the upper Coppercap and overlying formations. Some poles (P3) that postdate P2 poles and indicate high paleolatitudes are here interpreted as Late Precambrian. It is recorded in the ~ 1100 Ma Mamainse Point lavas (Robertson, 1973 ) and in dyke swarms of the Thunder Bay district (Pesonen, 1979) of the Keweenawan igneous Province of North America. There is strong evidence from dyke contact zones in the latter example that the dykes record a primary TRM. It is unclear (cf. Palmer, 1970; Robertson, 1973 and Halls and Pesonen, 1983 ) whether more than one rever- sal is present in the Mamainse succession. The consistency of repeated asymmetry through eight field reversals in the Gardar succession and the component structure of the remanence (first subsection of third section, Pesonen, 1979 and Thomas and Piper, 1991 ) demon- strate that a secondary component com- pounded with a primary antiparallel axis is not an adequate explanation of asymmetry. Geo- magnetic implications of this observation are discussed by Nevanelinna and Pesonen ( 1983 ). Because the younger units in the Gar- dar Province are magnetised predominantly with one polarity equivalent to the westerly declinations (it is not at present possible to identify unambiguously the normal or re- versed sense of this magnetisation with respect to the present field) asymmetry cannot be re- cognised at later times in this area. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: reversal is at least an incidental feature of the Upper Proterozoic geomagnetic field. It is recorded in the ~ 1100 Ma Mamainse Point lavas (Robertson, 1973 ) and in dyke swarms of the Thunder Bay district (Pesonen, 1979) of the Keweenawan igneous Province of North America. There is strong evidence from dyke contact zones in the latter example that the dykes record a primary TRM. It is unclear (cf. Palmer, 1970; Robertson, 1973 and Halls and Pesonen, 1983 ) whether more than one rever- sal is present in the Mamainse succession. The consistency of repeated asymmetry through eight field reversals in the Gardar succession and the component structure of the remanence (first subsection of third section, Pesonen, 1979 and Thomas and Piper, 1991 ) demon- strate that a secondary component com- pounded with a primary antiparallel axis is not an adequate explanation of asymmetry. Geo- magnetic implications of this observation are discussed by Nevanelinna and Pesonen ( 1983 ). Because the younger units in the Gar- dar Province are magnetised predominantly with one polarity equivalent to the westerly declinations (it is not at present possible to identify unambiguously the normal or re- versed sense of this magnetisation with respect to the present field) asymmetry cannot be re- cognised at later times in this area. An abundance of fresh gla- ciated exposure permitted an equitable spac- ing of cores (typically numbering 7-10) over several metres of outcrop at each site. In the laboratory samples were cut into 2.4 cm long cylinders. Magnetisations were measured be- fore and after alternating field (a.f.) and ther- mal treatment by 'minispin' and parastatic magnetometers. Cleaning steps by the a.f. method were 5 milliTesla (roT) to 30mT and then 10mT to peak fields of 140 mT. Cleaning steps by the thermal method were 100°C to 500°C and then in steps of 20 or 25°C to the Curie point of the magnetite (580°C) or he- matite (680 ° C) remanence carriers. Follow- ing examination of orthogonal vector projec- tions, components of magnetisation were resolved by principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980; Sherwood, 1989). With the exception of the lavas where the thermal method provided better component resolu- tion, both methods of treatment produced component definitions of comparable quality. Both earlier and later generations of the syenites have similar intensities of magnetisa- tion (Fig. 3). PIPER cord from this province (Halls and Pesonen, 1983) shows that only the return path of the loop (now referred to as the "Keweenawan Track" ) is recorded here. The extrapolation of this APW path backwards in time to ca. 1200 Ma, a period well defined by results from basic igneous suites, has remained unclear (see re- view by Roy, 1983 ). The Gardar Igneous Province of South Greenland, which forms the subject of this pa- per, is an example of a major rift-related ig- neous episode of Middle-Upper Proterozoic age. Whilst igneous activity was probably con- centrated in three short pulses (Blaxland et al., 1978), the collective palaeomagnetic results identify in outline a consistent pattern of APW between ca. 1300 and 1150 Ma (Piper, 1977a). When combined with data spanning the same interval from adjoining shield areas, they iden- tify an APW track which appears to be the pre- cursor of the path recognised in the Keweena- wan Province. Collectively these data define the pattern of continental movement over some 150 Ma of Proterozoic times (Piper, 1987).
